problem: Prior data-driven predictors of human perceptions of robot performance (e.g., random forests, GRUs) need hundreds of labeled episodes from user studies, which limits practical use. LLM-based prior work used narrative descriptions of interactions rather than raw sensor observations.
motivation: Querying people during interaction is disruptive, so robots need to infer subjective perceptions (competence, surprise, intent clarity) automatically to be evaluated and improved at scale. LLM world knowledge and in-context learning could make this sample-efficient without retraining, which matters in HRI where data is scarce.
key_idea: Use few-shot in-context learning of LLMs, prompted with string-serialized spatio-temporal robot, follower and pedestrian trajectories, to predict binary human perceptions of a guide robot, optionally with demonstrations drawn from the same user.
insight: With only K=4 demonstrations, Gemini and GPT ICL significantly outperform an RF trained on the same examples (e.g. Competence 0.67-0.72 vs 0.53), and zero-shot Gemini is significantly worse than ICL. Adding follower and pedestrian trajectories to robot trajectory and goal improves accuracy (RQ2 ablation). Just 4 personalized demonstrations improve accuracy further (Competence 0.67->0.76 at K=8, 0.72->0.79 at K=68). More non-personalized demonstrations bring only limited gains, probably because of long-context difficulties.
method: Problem formulation: episodes (person, observations, binary label) are collected at the end of each episode; the LLM predicts the label from the string-serialized query given instruction I plus demonstrations D≠ (other users) and/or D≈ (same user).

Observation encoding: an 8 s window at 1 Hz, in a robot-centric frame at t=0, with goal pose, robot trajectory, follower trajectory and pedestrians within 7.2 m; positions as (x,y), orientations as (cosθ,sinθ), undetected people marked 'unknown'.
Non-personalized ICL: K random demonstrations from training participants, balanced between positive and negative (K a power of 2, 4 to 64), with no fine-tuning; optional CoT prompt 'step by step'.
Personalized ICL: demonstrations from the same user as the evaluation example, either alone or combined with non-personalized ones (e.g. 4 personalized + 4 or 64 others).

SEAN TOGETHER v2 dataset: extends the original dataset from 235 episodes/45 participants to 404 episodes/69 participants, with 5-point Likert ratings binarized (4-5 positive, 1-2 negative, neutral dropped).

Evaluation protocol: participant-disjoint 40/40/20 split, balanced test set with one positive and one negative example per test participant, 25 repetitions with random demonstrations, linear mixed models with Tukey HSD.

setting.backbone: Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT 4.1 mini, Llama 3.2 90B (frozen, in-context learning); baselines RF and GRU trained from scratch
setting.model_size: Llama 3.2 90B; the others are not stated
setting.training_data: none for the LLMs (few-shot demonstrations of 4 to 68 episodes from SEAN TOGETHER v2, 404 episodes); RF and GRU are trained from scratch on the same demonstrations
setting.observation: Robot-frame trajectory features from Kinect people tracking and localization: goal pose, robot, follower and nearby pedestrian 2D positions and orientations over 8 s at 1 Hz, given as text
setting.action_space: not applicable (binary classification of perceived competence, surprise and intention)
setting.simulator: real world only (real-world dataset, not a navigation simulator)

numbers_note: The paper reports classification accuracy on a human-perception prediction task with its own dataset (SEAN TOGETHER v2), not on any listed navigation benchmark, so no benchmark entries were added.
results: Gemini 2.0 Flash and GPT 4.1 mini with ICL beat the RF at K=4, e.g. Competence 0.72 (Gemini CoT) vs 0.53 (RF), and at K=64 Gemini (0.73) still matches or exceeds RF (0.66). Adding 4 personalized demonstrations gives the best accuracy: Gemini reaches 0.79/0.76/0.75 (Competence/Surprise/Intention) at K=68 vs 0.72/0.70/0.69 without personalization. Llama 3.2 90B is close to chance.
limitations: Evaluated on a single robot-following task, with one robot and one campus setting, and only trajectory text with no multimodal input.

Accuracy gains from more non-personalized demonstrations are small or mixed (long-context issues), demonstrations are randomly sampled, and prompts need careful engineering (e.g. label semantics, goal-reached ambiguity).
Only binary labels and three perception dimensions; the test set is small (one positive and one negative example per test participant).
builds_on: Zhang et al. 2023 self-supervised perception prediction
